title: Briseno v. ConAgra Foods, Inc. (2017)
summary: The Ninth Circuit declined to add a freestanding administrative-feasibility requirement to Rule 23.
notes:
The opinion expressly identifies disagreement with the Third Circuit’s approach. This is not labeled a uniform Supreme Court rule.

The product was Wesson cooking oil labeled '100% Natural,' allegedly misleading because it contained genetically modified ingredients; the Ninth Circuit sided with the Sixth, Seventh and Eighth Circuits against the Third Circuit's administrative-feasibility requirement, reasoning that such a rule would effectively bar class actions over inexpensive consumer goods where no one keeps receipts.

sections.Parties: Purchasers of Wesson cooking oils sued ConAgra over the products’ 100% Natural labeling.
sections.Material Facts: The purchasers alleged that bioengineered ingredients made the label misleading and sought classes covering consumers in eleven states. ConAgra argued that consumers generally would not retain receipts and that there was no reliable, administratively feasible way to identify everyone who bought the products. The proposed definitions nevertheless used objective purchase and time-period criteria.
sections.Procedural History: The district court certified the classes without requiring a separate administrative-feasibility showing. The Ninth Circuit affirmed that approach.
sections.Issue: Must proponents of a Rule 23 class independently establish an administratively feasible way to identify class members?
sections.Holding: Not under the Ninth Circuit’s interpretation. The express requirements of Rule 23 provided the governing safeguards.
sections.Reasoning: The court began with Rule 23(a)’s stated prerequisites and the manageability component already present in Rule 23(b)(3). Adding a separate absolute requirement could make one consideration dispositive where the Rule called for balancing. The court also rejected the claim that due process demanded actual individual notice to everyone, emphasizing best practicable notice and later opportunities to challenge claims. Concerns about fraudulent claims and the defendant’s ability to contest purchases could be handled through administration and adjudication rather than automatically barring certification. The decision was particularly concerned with inexpensive consumer purchases for which individual litigation was unrealistic.

learning.why: The Ninth Circuit declined to add a freestanding administrative-feasibility requirement to Rule 23.

topics.cp-ascertainability: The Ninth Circuit rejected administrative feasibility as a freestanding additional prerequisite.
topics.cp-class-notice: Best practicable notice did not mean that every consumer must be individually identifiable.
topics.cp-rule-scope: Manageability and other express Rule 23 protections addressed the asserted policy concerns.
topics.cp-class-certification: The case holds that only Rule 23's express requirements govern certification, with no implied ascertainability showing.
topics.cp-frcp-23: The court reasoned from Rule 23's text and its manageability, notice and adequacy provisions.
